source.title: Med-SegLens: Latent-Level Model Diffing for Interpretable Medical Image Segmentation
source.authors: Salma J. Ahmed; Emad A. Mohammed; Azam Asilian Bidgoli

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes whether SAE latents serve as shared, stable representation units and reports that their overlap depends on cohort and their granularity changes with dictionary size. This refines the claim about SAE features as canonical units, but it does not test toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The study reports segmentation interventions and performance outcomes, but those results do not test the listed superposition or canonical-feature claims. The recorded rows are the reported cross-cohort latent overlap, dictionary-size effects on feature granularity, and bootstrap stability of latent alignment.
record.test_reason: The study uses BatchTopK SAE latents as the 'atomic units' for diffing segmentation models trained on different cohorts. It reports its own alignment method against baselines and latent-steering performance. It never tests whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical for a fixed model, for example across seeds or dictionary sizes with quantified overlap. The cross-cohort overlap compares different models trained on different data, so it measures representational similarity between models, not SAE canonicality. Bootstrap 'stability' scores how robust the matching is, not whether features are stable units. The dictionary-size remark is a qualitative hyperparameter-selection ablation with no number in the text. No toy models, neuron polysemanticity or LLMs are studied.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that latent-level diffing with SAEs reveals a shared, population-invariant backbone plus population-specific latents that act as causal bottlenecks under dataset shift. Targeted latent interventions recover about 70% of failure cases and raise edema Dice from 39.4% to 74.2% without retraining. They caveat that SAE latents depend on the training distribution and may be only partially interpreted.
record.recipe_differences: Uses BatchTopK SAEs and cross-dataset latent alignment in medical segmentation; it does not reproduce the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Cohort pair changes the fraction of shared latents. SAE expansion factor changes feature granularity and dead-feature rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Fraction of encoder/decoder-aligned SAE latents shared between SegFormers trained on different brain-MRI cohorts ranges from 19.2% (SSA–Healthy) to 58.9% (Adult–Pediatric).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently trained models on related data distributions learn partially shared, SAE-recoverable feature bases, with overlap scaling with data similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: Qualitatively, larger SAE dictionaries split features and leave more dead latents, while smaller ones give broader, entangled features. Figure 11 values are not given in the text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature granularity in vision segmentation models depends on dictionary size.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The reported alignment stability measures bootstrap consistency of matches, not semantic completeness or canonical identity. The paper acknowledges that latent features depend on training-data distributions and that interpretation can be partial or imperfect. The dictionary-size comparison is described qualitatively in the text; numerical figure values are not provided there.
record.rows_left_out: Segmentation intervention and performance results were omitted because they assess task correction, not whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical. Alignment metrics other than bootstrap stability were omitted because they assess alignment consistency, collisions, or predictability rather than feature-unit stability.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity-versus-dimension sweep or geometry analysis.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity-competition analysis.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity examined.
No LLMs; SAEs are applied to segmentation models as a tool, without testing whether features are spread across neurons.
No test of SAE completeness, of seed or run stability for a fixed model, or of quantified feature correspondence across dictionary sizes.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The study is an applied interpretability and model-diffing paper in medical segmentation; it cites Toy Models of Superposition only in related work. The reader's V5 links rested on conflating cross-model overlap and alignment-matching stability with SAE feature canonicality. The reader's supports and limits_scope labels are dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity versus dimension, overlap geometry, and sparsity-dependent transitions are not tested.
Neuron polysemanticity, capacity competition, and dedicated versus shared dimensions are not tested.
Alternative causes of polysemantic neurons are not tested.
The study concerns medical-image segmentation models, not LLMs; it does not test feature spreading across LLM neurons or LLM SAE recovery.
The study evaluates SAE latent alignment and interpretation, but does not establish semantic completeness or canonical identity across SAE training runs.
It represents SAE latents as individual coordinates but does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: SegFormer, Adult dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE dictionary expansion factors; the paper states that smaller dictionaries produce broader, less interpretable features.
rows.value: Smaller expansion factors produce broader, less interpretable features and partial feature entanglement.
rows.note: The paper does not give a numeric outcome for this qualitative comparison in the text.
rows.check: Hyperparameter-selection ablation, stated qualitatively. Figure 11 values cannot be read in the text, and feature identity across dictionary sizes is not compared. This is a selection value, not a test.

rows.subject: SegFormer, Adult dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE dictionary expansion factors; the paper describes 16 as the balance between reconstruction fidelity and interpretable, active features.
rows.value: An intermediate expansion factor of 16 provides the best trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and interpretable, active latent features.
rows.note: The paper does not give a numeric outcome for this qualitative comparison in the text.
rows.check: Selection value: the chosen expansion factor of 16. Not a result on V5.

rows.subject: SegFormer, Adult dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE dictionary expansion factors; the paper states that larger dictionaries encourage feature splitting.
rows.value: Larger expansions encourage feature splitting, at the cost of a substantially higher fraction of dead features.
rows.note: The paper does not give a numeric outcome for this qualitative comparison in the text.
rows.check: Qualitative remark that larger dictionaries cause feature splitting and more dead features. No quantified feature correspondence across sizes; this is a selection ablation.

rows.subject: SegFormer and U-Net
rows.operation_detail: Interpreted SAE latents by semantic category and reported that multiple latents represent each tumor or anatomical category, varying in location, morphology, scale, and depth.

conditions.value: Multiple datasets; examples include tumor and healthy anatomy

rows.value: Multiple latents emerge for each tumor or anatomical category, capturing variation in spatial location, morphology, scale, and depth.
rows.note: This reports fine-grained decomposition, but does not test feature completeness or a canonical ground-truth set.
rows.check: Qualitative report that several latents map to each class. It does not measure completeness, stability or canonicality.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Bootstrap stability of latent matching for Adult–Pediatric, Adult–SSA, and Adult–IXI under the reported alignment methods
reader_labels.reason: Reported matching stability is 98.1–100.0 across these settings, supporting reproducibility of the aligned correspondences under bootstrap resampling (r11–r22). This does not establish semantic completeness or canonicality.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Shared-latent fractions vary across cohort pairs, and changing dictionary expansion changes feature granularity, so the results do not establish a single complete, canonical feature set (r1–r9).
